name: THE THREE CHEEKS TO THE WIND BURGER (comes with guaniciale)

recipe.history:
Guanciale — from the Italian guancia, meaning cheek — is cured pig jowl, and it is one of the most revered and ancient cured meats in the Italian larder. Unlike pancetta, which is cured belly, or bacon, which is smoked and comes predominantly from the back and belly, guanciale is cut from the jowl and neck of the pig — a region dense with fat-marbled, intensely flavored meat that yields a product richer, silkier, and more deeply porky than almost anything else the animal offers. Its history is rooted in the peasant cuisines of central Italy, particularly Lazio and Umbria, where no part of the slaughtered pig was wasted. The jowl was rubbed with salt, black pepper, and sometimes chili, then hung in cool cellars to cure for a minimum of three weeks, often longer, until the fat turned translucent and the flavor concentrated into something almost sweet and nutty beneath its heat. Guanciale is the non-negotiable, traditional fat source for two of Rome's most iconic pasta dishes — carbonara and amatriciana — and using anything else in either dish will earn you the quiet, permanent contempt of every Roman who has ever lived.

Guanciale's entry into the American culinary consciousness was slow and largely mediated by the Italian-American community's gradual shift from grocery-store approximations back toward artisanal authenticity. For much of the twentieth century, domestic cured meats were dominated by commercially produced bacon and pancetta, and guanciale was nearly impossible to source outside of specialty Italian importers or the home curing operations maintained by immigrant families. The craft charcuterie movement of the early 2000s changed everything — as American butchers began learning old-world curing techniques, guanciale became a calling card of seriousness in professional kitchens. By the mid-2010s, it had made its inevitable leap onto the gourmet burger circuit, where its intense rendered fat — which liquefies at a lower temperature than pancetta or bacon and pools around the meat in glossy, fragrant sheets — proved to be one of the most transformative single toppings a burger could receive.

The first time I cooked guanciale I was working a line station at a small Italian restaurant that took its cured meats with a level of seriousness that bordered on religious. The chef handed me a slab and told me to render it in a dry pan — no oil, nothing — just medium-low heat and patience. I watched it go from a firm, white-and-pink block to something trembling and translucent, the fat running off it in clear rivulets that smelled of black pepper and time and something almost floral. The crisp edge and yielding center, that contrast, made me eat a strip standing over the stove like a criminal. The chef saw me and said nothing, which in that kitchen was the highest form of approval. I have been chasing that precise first bite every time I cook guanciale since.

The imperative to cook a burger to medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — is inseparable from the question of fat, and guanciale makes this argument more eloquently than almost any other topping. The rendered fat from slowly crisped guanciale mingles with the pink, freely running juices of a medium-rare patty, and the combination on the palate is a lesson in how great cooking works: richness meeting richness, each amplifying the other, nothing dried out, nothing wasted. Cook that same patty to well done and the fat from the guanciale has nowhere to go, nothing to marry with, no juice to mingle into — it pools on a dry gray disc and the whole enterprise becomes sad. Medium rare is not a temperature. It is a philosophy of generosity toward the ingredient, a refusal to punish good meat with unnecessary heat, a commitment to letting the best version of a thing be itself.
ingredients: 4 large eggs (3 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
6 tablespoons unsalted butter, softened and cubed
8 oz guanciale, sliced 1/8-inch thick (about 18 to 20 slices)
Pinch of crushed red pepper flakes
2 cloves garlic, minced to a paste
3 large yellow onions, halved and thinly sliced
2 oz Pecorino Romano, shaved with a vegetable peeler
instructions: 1. MAKE THE BRIOCHE BUNS — DAY BEFORE: Combine warm milk, yeast, and 1 teaspoon of the sugar in the bowl of a stand mixer. Let stand 5 to 8 minutes until foamy.
2. Add flour, remaining sugar, salt, and 3 eggs. Mix on low with the dough hook 2 minutes until just combined, then increase to medium and mix 6 minutes.
3. Add softened butter one cube at a time on medium speed, incorporating fully between additions, about 8 to 10 minutes total. Increase to medium-high and mix 6 to 8 minutes until smooth and elastic.
4. Transfer to a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and refrigerate overnight (8 to 12 hours).
5. Next day, divide dough into 6 equal portions. Shape into tight round balls. Place on parchment-lined baking sheet. Cover and proof 2 to 3 hours at room temperature.
6. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush buns with egg wash (1 egg beaten with 1 tablespoon water). Bake 16 to 18 minutes until deep golden brown. Cool completely on a wire rack.

7. MAKE THE CARAMELIZED ONIONS: Melt butter with olive oil in a wide, heavy skillet over medium-low heat. Add onions and salt. Cook, stirring every 5 to 8 minutes, for 45 to 55 minutes until deeply golden, jammy, and sweet. Add thyme and white wine in the last 5 minutes. Stir to incorporate and cook off the wine. Set aside.

8. MAKE THE BLACK PEPPER AIOLI: Whisk egg yolks and mustard in a medium bowl. Whisk in garlic paste. Add neutral oil in a very slow stream, drop by drop at first, whisking constantly until the emulsion thickens. Continue adding oil in a thin drizzle, then whisk in olive oil. Whisk in white wine vinegar. Season with coarse black pepper and kosher salt. Refrigerate until needed.

9. RENDER THE GUANCIALE: Lay guanciale slices in a single layer in a cold skillet. Place over medium-low heat. Season with black pepper and red pepper flakes. Cook slowly, 6 to 8 minutes, turning occasionally, until the fat is rendered and the edges are golden and crisp but the centers remain slightly soft and yielding. Transfer to a paper-towel-lined plate. Reserve the rendered fat in the pan.

10. FORM THE PATTIES: Gently combine ground chuck and ground brisket in a large bowl. Season with salt and pepper. Form into 6 patties, approximately 4 1/2 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick, with a shallow center dimple. Refrigerate 20 minutes.

11. COOK THE PATTIES: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking (or use the guanciale pan with reserved rendered fat). Cook patties without pressing, 3 minutes on the first side until a deep brown crust forms.
12. Flip once. Cook 2 to 2 1/2 minutes more. Check internal temperature — target 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. Transfer to a wire rack and rest 3 minutes.
13. TOAST THE BUNS: Split buns and toast cut-side down in a hot dry skillet 60 to 90 seconds until golden.
14. ASSEMBLE: Spread black pepper aioli generously on both cut sides of the bun. Place arugula on the bottom bun. Add the rested patty.
15. Spoon a generous mound of caramelized onions over the patty. Arrange 3 to 4 slices of rendered guanciale over the onions.
16. Drape shaved Pecorino Romano over the guanciale. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt. Close with the top bun and serve immediately.
